source.title: Asymptotics of Ridge(less) Regression under General Source Condition
source.authors: Dominic Richards; Jaouad Mourtada; L. Rosasco

record.tranche_reason: The study's own asymptotic analysis reports additional peaks in ridgeless bias and variance beyond the interpolation threshold, refining the shape claim for a structured linear-regression setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a theoretical risk characterization and Figure 3 curves for ridgeless bias and variance. Those component curves are not a reported total test-error curve. Double-descent results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper's asymptotic theory, checked by simulations, shows extra peaks in the ridgeless bias and variance beyond the interpolation threshold, at n = d1. This bears on V6's claim that the peak can split into several peaks. It also shows the bias peak arises from parameter–covariance misalignment rather than label noise. The setting is linear ridge(less) regression, not deep networks, and only error components are plotted.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The main conclusion is a precise asymptotic risk formula for ridge regression under a general source condition. In the strong/weak features model, ridgeless interpolation can be optimal among ridge estimators at finite SNR when strong features carry more signal. Noisy weak features act as regularisation. Additional peaks in ridgeless bias and variance can occur beyond the interpolation threshold, located at n = d1 and depending on feature structure.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses asymptotic random-matrix analysis of ridge and ridgeless linear regression with structured covariance and parameter source conditions, rather than the original deep-network size and epoch experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported peak locations depend on the number of strong and weak features, ambient dimension, coefficient alignment, and eigenvalue ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: In the overparameterised regime, zero regularisation (interpolation) can be optimal among ridge estimators at finite SNR, when signal concentrates on high-variance directions (Corollary 2, Fig. 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal ridge penalty can be zero for overparameterised linear regression when the true parameter is aligned with principal components.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding noisy weak features acts as implicit regularisation. With tuned eigenvalue ratio, it recovers optimally tuned ridge on the strong features (Fig. 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Added noise features implicitly regularise ridgeless regression.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics
record.problems: The results concern an asymptotic, structured linear-regression model, not deep networks. Figure 3 reports bias and variance components rather than a total test-error curve; its plotted values are figure-only, and no uncertainty bars are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional Figure 3 rows were extracted: the plotted curves have multiple settings, but the flattened legend does not reliably assign every parameter combination to each curve. The text's explicit peak findings are represented in r1 and r2.

untested.parts: Whether the extra peaks disappear under optimally tuned ridge is not shown; optimal ridge is only plotted against eigenvalue ratio at γ = 3.5 (Fig. 1). Label-noise level is not varied as a driver of the peaks.
No deep networks; no model-size sweep.
No sample-size sweep at fixed model; the authors say γ should not be read as overparameterisation.
Only γ ≥ 1 is plotted, and only bias and variance components; no total-risk curve across the interpolation threshold.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this paper. The authors caution that γ = d/n changes the data distribution and is not a degree of overparameterisation. Figure 3 covers only γ ≥ 1 and plots components, not total risk.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report a total test-error fall-rise-fall curve as model size grows.
The paper does not sweep sample size near the interpolation threshold while holding the model setting fixed.
The paper studies ridge regression, but does not report a total-risk curve demonstrating improvement again as capacity grows past interpolation across model classes.
The paper does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.

The paper reports additional peaks in ridgeless bias and variance and identifies feature-structure conditions for them. It does not test whether label noise causes the peaks or whether peaks disappear under optimally tuned regularization.
The paper does not compare the curve with an effective-parameter count.

conditions.value: strong and weak features; ψ1 = 0.35 in Figure 3
various eigenvalue ratios ρ1/ρ2 and coefficient ratios φ1/φ2

rows.measure: Ridgeless bias component of test error
rows.note: The authors state that an additional peak occurs in ridgeless bias beyond the interpolation threshold, in the hard setting when n = d1. Figure 3 shows curves for various feature settings.
rows.check: The extra bias peak at n = d1 appears only in the 'hard' setting (φ1/φ2 < 1); the isotropic curve shows none. It is a component of test error, not the total risk. The bias term carries no noise σ², so this peak is not noise-driven. Values are figure-only; theory curves are checked against simulations (d = 2^8, 20 replications).

rows.measure: Ridgeless variance component of test error
rows.note: The authors state that a variance peak occurs when n = d1 and ρ1 > ρ2. Figure 3 shows curves for various feature settings.
rows.check: The extra variance peak at n = d1 appears only when ρ1/ρ2 is large (300 in Figure 3), not at ρ1/ρ2 = 1. It is a component curve, not total risk; values are figure-only. The authors note this variance peak could have been derived from prior work [16].

source_check.problem: The variance panel varies ψ1, including 0.65, despite the caption's blanket ψ1 = 0.35.
